content: Potassium sulfide is a chemical compound with the molecular formula K₂S. It is classified as an inorganic polymer and exhibits an antifluorite structure. This structural arrangement means that the smaller potassium ions (K⁺) occupy the tetrahedral sites typically associated with fluoride ions (F⁻) in fluorite, while the larger sulfide ions (S²⁻) occupy the eight-coordinate sites usually associated with calcium ions (Ca²⁺). Compounds such as lithium sulfide (Li₂S), sodium sulfide (Na₂S), and rubidium sulfide (Rb₂S) crystallize in a similar manner. This salt contains the highly basic sulfide anion (S²⁻), which undergoes complete hydrolysis in water according to the following reaction: S²⁻ + H₂O → SH⁻ + OH⁻. For many practical purposes, this reaction is not significant because the resulting mixture of hydrogen sulfide ions (SH⁻) and hydroxide ions (OH⁻) behaves as a source of sulfide ions (S²⁻). Other alkali metal sulfides exhibit similar behavior. Potassium sulfide is typically synthesized through the reaction of elemental potassium with sulfur. In laboratory settings, this synthesis is often carried out in a solution of anhydrous ammonia. Sulfurated potash, also known as liver of sulfur, is a poorly defined mixture that includes potassium sulfide, potassium polysulfide, potassium thiosulfate, and possibly potassium bisulfide. Synonyms for this mixture include hepar sulfuris, liver of sulfur, sulfurated potash, and sulfurated potassa. Liver of sulfur is primarily used in metalworking to create a patina, which imparts a brown coloration to copper alloys. Historically, liver of sulfur was also used in pharmaceutical preparations, such as white lotion. At one time, sulfurated potash was employed as a treatment for arthritis. However, its use fell out of favor due to the toxic nature of sulfides and polysulfides. Potassium sulfides are formed as byproducts when black powder is burned. These compounds play a critical role as intermediates in various pyrotechnic effects, such as those seen in senko hanabi (Japanese sparklers) and certain glitter formulations. Potassium sulfide is not directly added to fireworks; instead, it forms during the combustion process.
